content: Dental floss is a tool designed to remove food particles and dental plaque from the surfaces of teeth. It is typically made from either thin nylon filaments or a plastic material such as Teflon or polyethylene. The floss is carefully inserted between the teeth and moved along the sides of the teeth, particularly near the gumline, to clean these areas effectively. Dental floss is available in various forms, including flavored or unflavored, and waxed or unwaxed varieties. The invention of dental floss is attributed to Levi Spear Parmly, a dentist from New Orleans, who began recommending the use of silk floss for cleaning teeth as early as 1815. However, it was not commercially available until 1882, when the Codman and Shurtleff company began producing unwaxed silk floss for consumer use. In 1898, Johnson & Johnson received the first patent for dental floss. Early brands included Red Cross, Salter Sill Co., and Brunswick. The practice of flossing was even mentioned in James Joyce's novel Ulysses (serialized between 1918 and 1920), marking an early reference to flossing in literature. Despite its introduction, flossing was not widely adopted until after World War II, when Dr. Charles C. Bass developed nylon floss. Nylon proved superior to silk due to its greater resistance to abrasion and improved elasticity. Today, dentists and dental hygienists strongly advocate for daily oral hygiene routines that include both brushing and flossing. While nearly all Americans brush their teeth, only about 12% floss daily, 39% floss less frequently, and 49% do not floss at all, according to the American Dental Association (ADA). Dental floss is typically packaged in plastic dispensers containing 10 to 50 meters of floss. Users pull out the desired length of floss and sever it against a small protected blade within the dispenser. The floss is then held between the fingers for use. However, maintaining a firm grip on the floss can be challenging due to the tension required to maneuver it between tight teeth and the slipperiness caused by saliva. To improve handling, the floss can be wrapped around one or both fingers, ideally above the first joint, to allow for a traditional pinch grip with the thumb. Care must be taken not to wrap the floss too tightly, as this can restrict circulation. When switching to a fresh segment of floss, it is advisable to loosen the wrap to avoid excessive tension. Alternatively, tying the ends of the floss together to form a loop can make it easier to handle, even in wet conditions, and reduce pressure on the skin. Rotating the loop allows for the use of a clean section of floss for each tooth, minimizing the risk of transferring plaque bacteria between teeth. Specialized plastic wands are also available to hold the floss, which can make it easier to reach the back teeth, though they may limit the angles achievable compared to manual flossing. The proper technique for flossing involves gently sliding the floss between the teeth to remove food particles and plaque. Ideally, the floss should be curved into a C-shape around each tooth and moved away from the gumline to scrape the tooth's surface. This method can clean both the front and back of the tooth. Moving the floss from below the gumline to above it helps remove plaque from both above and below the gumline. Improper or infrequent flossing can lead to bleeding gums, often caused by gingival inflammation due to gingivitis. The ADA recommends flossing at least once daily. Incorrect or overly aggressive flossing can contribute to tooth decay. To floss effectively, the floss should be curved against the side of the tooth in a C-shape and wiped from under the gumline to the tip of the tooth two or three times. This process should be repeated for adjacent teeth and all other teeth in the mouth. It is important to note that dental floss does not clean the concave interproximal areas beneath the contact points of teeth. For optimal results, using mouthwash after flossing, especially if gums bleed, is recommended. Some power flossers incorporate vibration, which is transferred through the floss from its ends. This innovation is likely inspired by the use of vibration in modern electric toothbrushes. The subtle movement caused by vibration allows the floss to navigate the path of least resistance when pressed between teeth. It also temporarily separates the tooth and gum, facilitating easier penetration below the gumline with less force. This increased control reduces the risk of the floss popping through the teeth and causing painful gum trauma. Vibrations are often considered soothing and can massage the gumline, much like electric toothbrushes provide comfort to teeth and gums. Vibrating floss is less likely to cause cuts or abrasions, as the pressure is more evenly distributed, allowing for better adaptation of the gum tissue. Flossing, when combined with regular toothbrushing, is highly effective in preventing gum disease, bad breath (halitosis), and dental caries.
